text: Sheath blight (ចំនួរលាកស្រទាប្ស្លិក, "chomngu roleak srotoap sleuk") is caused by the soil-borne fungus Rhizoctonia solani. Oval lesions with a grayish-white center and brown border form on the leaf sheath near the waterline, then enlarge and spread upward onto the sheath and leaf blade, killing sheaths and leaves as they go. Under humid, densely-planted, heavily nitrogen-fertilized conditions the lesions merge and the disease can climb high up the plant, weakening stems (raising lodging risk near harvest) and causing poor grain fill. The fungus survives between seasons as hard resting structures (sclerotia) in the soil and old stubble, so it tends to recur on the same fields year after year if residue isn't managed. Management: avoid overly dense spacing and excess nitrogen, improve field drainage/aeration on fields where this is a chronic problem, and clear and destroy infected stubble rather than leaving it in the field or floating on standing water, where it can reinfect the next crop.
